_note: Generated by scripts/build_daily_topics.py. One topic per day, same for email, Instagram and the Facebook group. Cycle = len(topics) days, no repeats inside a cycle.

topics.title: The brand core
topics.why: Your brand core is a one-page summary of who you are. Everything you write and post comes from it. Brands without one often end up competing on price and discounts. Brands with one need fewer discounts, because trust does the selling.
steps: Describe 2 or 3 types of customer. Note their goals, what bugs them and where they spend time online.
Write your brand promise in one sentence (why choose us).
Pick three words for your personality and three words you never use.
Write two or three values, each with one thing you actually do that proves it.
Write your story in under 100 words: why the brand exists. Then save all five answers on one page.
results: You have 2 or 3 short customer descriptions.
You have one promise sentence.
You have a six-word voice guide.
Every value has proof, not just a claim.
A one-page brand core is saved where your team, freelancers and AI tools can read it.

topics.title: Customer profiles
topics.why: A customer profile describes one type of buyer. Built from real customer words, it tells you what to say in ads, pages and emails. Built from guesses, it sends you the wrong way.
steps: Collect 30 to 50 real customer quotes. Use reviews, a short survey and support emails (SOP 16 shows how).
For one profile, write their age range and stage of life. Then write the job they "hire" your product to do: the problem it solves.
Add their top 3 objections and the exact words they use for the problem and the product.
Add where they shop and what they compare you with.
results: You have a document of real quotes.
The profile has a who and a why.
The profile has phrases you can copy straight into ads.
You know your real competitors and channels for this profile. Repeat for each profile.

topics.title: Brand guidelines
topics.why: Brand guidelines are a short guide anyone can follow: a freelancer, a creator or an AI tool. People recognise a brand after seeing it many times looking the same way. Guidelines make that happen without you checking everything.
steps: Add your logo versions and the empty space to leave around them.
Add your main and extra colours with their hex codes (for example #0B1F3A), and your fonts and sizes.
Describe your photo and video style: lighting, framing and props, with 3 example images.
Add good and bad examples of your voice. Add do and don't examples for ads, emails and social posts.
results: The page shows each logo with a clear-space rule.
Anyone can match your colours and type exactly.
A freelancer could shoot on-brand content from the page alone.
The guide is finished and shared as one link or PDF.

topics.title: Why your profile is part of every ad
topics.why: Many people who see an ad do not click it. They tap your name to check you out first. If they find three old posts, no reviews and a broken link, they leave. A strong profile makes every ad dollar work harder, for free.
steps: Open your Instagram, TikTok and Facebook profiles on your phone as a stranger would. Log out or use a private window.
Check each profile does three jobs. It proves you are real, shows what you sell and gives a clear next step.
Fix the biggest gap on each profile using the checklist in Lesson 4.2.
results: You see each profile the way an ad viewer does.
You have a list of which job each profile fails.
Every profile does all three jobs.

topics.title: Profile checklist (Instagram, TikTok, Facebook)
topics.why: A profile is a mini landing page. Fourteen checks on each platform make sure it builds trust and matches what your ads promise.
steps: Go through every row of the checklist in the table below on Instagram.
Repeat the checklist on TikTok and Facebook.
Check that the product, offer and look in your ads also show on each profile. For example: "free shipping this week".
results: Each Instagram item is ticked or fixed.
All three profiles pass the checklist.
Ads and profiles tell the same story, so trust does not drop when people tap through.

topics.title: Why creative is the targeting now
topics.why: Creative means the ad itself: the picture or video plus the words. Ad platforms like Meta now find the buyers for you, so your creative decides who stops to look. A wide audience with many different ads usually beats a narrow audience with one style of ad.
steps: Open Meta Ads Manager and go to the Ads tab. Count how many different ads are live right now (different ideas, not just new sizes).
Check that your main ad set for new people uses a broad audience. That means Advantage+ audience, or just country and age, not a stack of interests.
Set a goal for a steady flow of new ads. For example: 4 to 8 new ads every two weeks.
results: You have a count. As a rough guide, fewer than 6 live ideas means the account is short of creative.
Your targeting is wide and your ads do the targeting.
You have a written creative volume target. Lesson 5.2 shows how to hit it.

topics.title: The creative management cycle
topics.why: Making ads works best as a loop you repeat every week or two. Each turn of the loop makes the next batch smarter, because winners teach you why they won.
steps: Research: spend 20 minutes reading reviews and comments. Browse rivals' ads in the Meta Ad Library (facebook.com/ads/library) and note trends.
Plan: pick the pillar (topic), the angle (reason to buy) and the one thing you will test.
Brief: write one page per concept (ad idea) using the template in Lesson 7.9.
Produce: make the ads yourself, with creators or with AI editing tools.
Launch: put the new ads live as a batch, not one at a time.
Learn: after 7 days, score each ad and write one line on why each winner won.
results: You have 3 to 5 notes on what buyers say and what others run.
You have a one-line test, for example "Prove pillar, durability angle, testing review-led hook vs demo hook".
Each concept has a brief anyone can produce from.
You have finished files in 4:5 and 9:16 sizes.
All new ads start on the same day so they are judged fairly.
Your next brief starts from written learnings, not guesses.

topics.title: Why other people's faces sell your product
topics.why: People trust people more than brands. When someone like your customer explains why they switched, it feels more real than a brand praising itself. It also gives ad platforms the mix of ages, styles and reasons they need to find new buyers. UGC (user-generated content) means photos and videos made by customers or creators instead of the brand.
steps: Read the four ways to work with creators in the table below. They are gifting, paid UGC, influencer or partnership, and affiliate.
Start with gifting and paid UGC. Send product to 10 creators and pay 2 or 3 for videos ready for ads.
Keep working with the creators whose videos perform, and move the best ones up to paid partners.
results: You know what each costs and what you get.
You have your first creator videos to test.
Your creator roster grows from proven performers.

topics.title: Finding the right creators
topics.why: Fit matters more than follower count. A creator with 4,000 engaged followers who already talks about your kind of product beats a 400,000-follower lifestyle account.
steps: Search your own tags and mentions on Instagram and TikTok for customers who already post about you.
Search the platforms for the problems your product solves, not your product name. Save creators you would stop to watch.
Use Instagram's creator marketplace (in Meta Business Suite) and TikTok One (formerly TikTok Creator Marketplace). Filter by audience location, size and category. Check who makes content for rivals.
Score each one out of 10. Look at comfort on camera and speaking to your customer. Check natural style, a real community in comments, regular posting and shared values.
Shortlist creators who score 7 or more.
results: You have a list of warm creator leads.
Your list grows with problem-focused creators.
You have 20 or more candidates.
Each creator has a score.
You have a focused shortlist to contact.

topics.title: Numbers first
topics.why: Learn the five numbers that say if an ad makes or loses money. Only then open Ads Manager. They come from Module 1 and Helix works them out from your daily numbers. With them, every later decision is a simple comparison.
steps: Open the Dashboard on Month. Copy your target MER, break-even ROAS (sales for each $1 of ads) and break-even CPA from the cards.
Work out your target CPA across all ads: AOV times target MER. Cold campaigns may cost up to double that, as the table below shows.
Compare your target CPA with what similar stores pay to win a customer. If yours is lower, do not spend yet: fix offer, order size or margins first (Module 2).
results: You have three numbers written on your campaign brief.
You have a target CPA and a cold CPA allowance.
You know whether your numbers can support paid ads today.

topics.title: Testing campaigns vs scaling campaigns
topics.why: Keeping testing and winning separate stops new tests from upsetting what already works. Three kinds of campaign do the job: scaling, testing and build.
steps: Create a build campaign that is always switched off, and build each new ad there once.
Make a testing campaign (or test ad set) with 20 to 30% of the budget. Put each new batch of ads there.
Keep proven ads in scaling campaigns with 70 to 80% of the budget. Do not add new ads to them while they are winning.
When a test ad wins, copy it into a scaling campaign with Use existing post. That way it keeps its post ID, likes and comments.
results: You have a paused campaign holding every ad you have made.
New ads get a fixed, fair budget away from your winners.
Scaling campaigns stay stable.
The winner runs in scaling with its social proof intact.

topics.title: Find your way around Ads Manager
topics.why: Ads Manager looks busy, but you only use a handful of parts. Once you know what each one is for, it stops being scary. It becomes a simple table you check for 5 minutes a day.
steps: Open Ads Manager (adsmanager.facebook.com, or Meta Business Suite > All tools > Ads Manager). Check the ad account name at the top left.
Set the date range at the top right to Last 7 days.
Click Columns and choose your Daily preset (or Performance if you have not made one yet).
Click the Campaigns tab, then click a campaign name to open it. Look at the three levels (campaign, ad set, ad), but do not change anything. Close it with X or Close.
results: You are in your store's ad account.
The table shows the last week.
You see Results, Cost per result, Amount spent and ROAS.
You know where the budget, the audience and the ads live.

topics.title: Account setup checklist
topics.why: Ten minutes of setup before you spend money stops the most costly Meta problems. These are lost sales tracking, hacked accounts and spending that runs away. Do it once, one step at a time, and check it again every quarter.
steps: Go to business.facebook.com/settings and click Users > People, then Invite people. Invite a second person you trust with Full control (Meta's name for admin).
In the same Business Settings, open Security Centre. Switch on Two-factor authentication for everyone: a code from your phone as well as a password.
Still in Security Centre, click Start verification. Enter your legal business name, address, phone and website, exactly as on your official records (see Meta: verify your business).
Add the Facebook & Instagram sales channel in Shopify.
Turn data sharing up to Maximum.
Open Events Manager (All tools > Events Manager) and click your pixel. Look at the Purchase row in the Overview tab.
results: People lists two people with full control.
Security Centre shows two-factor required for all admins.
Verification shows "In review" or "Verified". If you see "Ineligible for verification" or no button, you do not need it yet. Skip it and come back later.
Facebook & Instagram appears under Sales channels, with your business, ad account, Page and pixel connected. See Shopify: set up Facebook & Instagram.
Data sharing reads "Maximum".
Purchase shows events from both Browser and Server, in your store's currency. If it shows nothing, place a small test order and check again in an hour.

topics.title: Before you launch: tracking you can trust
topics.why: Bad data leads to bad decisions, and a broken pixel can make good ads look like failures. Check tracking once now, then every month. Your store's own reports are the truth; ad platforms are only for direction.
steps: Add the Facebook & Instagram sales channel in Shopify. Connect your business account, ad account, page and pixel (see Shopify: Facebook and Instagram).
Set data sharing to Maximum to turn on server events.
Install the Google & YouTube app and connect Merchant Center, Google Ads and GA4 (see Shopify: Google).
Check privacy and cookie settings in Settings > Customer privacy (see Shopify: customer events).

Open Meta Events Manager and Google Ads Goals > Conversions. Check that the pixel (or Google tag) and server events are connected through your store. Server events are the Conversions API on Meta and enhanced conversions on Google.
Make Purchase the only primary (main) conversion for sales campaigns, with add to cart and others as secondary.
results: The sales channel shows all four connected.
Sales reach Meta even when a browser blocks the pixel.
Google receives your products and purchases.
Consent is handled for your markets.
Both show purchases from browser and server.
Only Purchase is primary on each platform.

topics.title: Setting up target audiences
topics.why: Audiences tell each platform who already knows you. Then cold campaigns find new people and warm campaigns reach the right ones. Set them up once on Meta, Google and TikTok, then reuse them in every campaign.
steps: On Meta, set audience groups for the whole account in Advertising settings > Audience segments (under All tools). Add your engaged audience (visitors and social engagers) and existing customers (customer list or store link).
On Meta, click Audiences, then Create audience, then Custom audience, once for each.
On Meta, build lookalikes of buyers or best customers. Make them at 1%, 3 to 5% and 10% for later tests.

Set cold targeting to broad: your country and age 18 to 65+. Pick all genders unless the product is clearly for one. Choose who to leave out of cold ads: nobody, recent buyers, or all buyers and engagers. Meta announced in 2025 it is retiring its old past-customer spend cap, so check Ads Manager for your account. To keep past buyers out of cold ads, exclude your customer audiences. Then watch the Audience segments breakdown.
On Google, give it signals and words to avoid.
On TikTok, copy the same layers.
results: Reports show how much spend reaches brand-new people.
Every custom audience shows "Ready".
Three lookalike sizes are ready.
Cold campaigns reach new people on purpose.
Google has signals to guide it and words to avoid.
TikTok has the same audience layers as Meta.

topics.title: Find your way around Google Ads
topics.why: Google Ads hides a lot behind menus. You only need a few screens: campaigns, search terms, conversions and recommendations.
steps: Open ads.google.com and check the account name and ID (top of the page) is your store's account.
Click Campaigns in the left menu and set the date range (top right) to Last 7 days.
Show sales value in your table.
Click Insights and reports > Search terms to see what people typed before clicking your ads.
results: You are in the right account.
The table shows last week's campaigns.
You can see sales and ROAS for each campaign.
You know where to find wasted searches each week.

topics.title: Foundations
topics.why: A clean Google foundation means every dollar is tracked and nothing changes without you. Do this once before you spend money, tick each step, and recheck tracking monthly.
steps: In Google Ads, open Admin > Access and security. Check that you (not an agency) are an admin owner of the account.
In Shopify, install the Google & YouTube app. Connect your Google Ads account and Merchant Center (where Google keeps your product list, called a feed).
Tell Google that a purchase is the only thing that counts.
Connect Google Analytics 4 (GA4) to Shopify and Google Ads.
In Tools > Shared library > Audience manager, build site visitors, buyers and your email list (customer match).
In Google Ads open Recommendations, click Auto-apply (top right) and untick every auto-applied recommendation.
results: Your own email is listed with Admin access. If an agency owns it, ask them in writing to transfer ownership to you.
The app shows both accounts connected and products syncing.
Only Purchase is marked Primary, and enhanced conversions show "Active".
GA4 shows purchases, and Google Ads lists GA4 as linked (see Google: link Google Ads and Analytics).
Three audiences show in Audience manager.
Google cannot change your campaigns without your click.

topics.title: TikTok readiness
topics.why: TikTok can bring cheap attention. But only once you have videos that work there and tracking in place. Getting ready first stops you paying to learn what free posts could teach you. Only start TikTok ads once Meta and Google are profitable.
steps: Post free TikTok videos 3 to 5 times a week for a month. Learn what works for you.
Save the 10 to 15 best videos that are good enough to run as ads.
Make a TikTok Business Center and an ad account. Install the TikTok pixel through the TikTok app in Shopify (it reports views, carts and sales).
Make a simple view in TikTok Ads Manager.
results: You know which video styles get views and comments.
You have a bank of ad-ready videos.
TikTok Events Manager shows Purchase events coming in. Older setups may call it Complete payment (see TikTok: updated standard events).
One saved view shows every number you need.

topics.title: Optimising TikTok
topics.why: TikTok ads can tire within days, so they need closer watching than Meta. Early signs warn you before cost per sale gets worse.
steps: Check TikTok every day or two. Watch for early warning signs. Cost per click goes up, cost per add to cart goes up, or fewer people watch the videos.
Turn off ads that eat budget with a poor cost per sale.
Did cost per sale go up after you turned off an earlier-step campaign (like add to cart)? Turn it back on.
When things work, grow one move at a time.
Start TikTok at about 10% of your total ad budget (a rule of thumb). Judge it by your total MER on the Dashboard (total ad spend as a share of total sales).
results: You spot tired ads before CPA rises.
Spend moves to working ads.
TikTok gets the data it needs again.
Growth comes from new creative and campaigns, not just more budget.
You see TikTok's effect on the whole store.

topics.title: Why build the list
topics.why: Your email and SMS list is an audience you own and can reach for free, any time. Each engaged subscriber earns a little every month. Collect emails when ads are cheap, and sell when ads are costly. It is one of the most reliable ways to grow.
steps: Check your list size and the share engaged in the last 90 days in your email app.
Set a list growth target for the next quiet months, for example +2,000 subscribers before October.
Plan one list-building push (form upgrade, competition or lead ads) in a month when ads are cheap.
results: You know your owned audience size today.
You have a written target with a date.
The push is on your calendar.

topics.title: Running a competition
topics.why: Running a competition well is a seven-part job, from rules to measuring who buys. Skipping the follow-up flow wastes most of the value.
steps: Pick the type and prize, and check your local promotion rules (some places need a permit).
Build the entry form on a store page and as a pop-up.
Make the content: a prize image, a short video and clear steps to enter.
Run ads to broad audiences with a Leads campaign. Or use a Sales campaign that sends people to the entry page.
Set up a welcome flow for entrants with a small offer.
After the draw, announce the winner and send everyone else a "sorry you didn't win" offer.
results: You know the competition is legal where you run it.
People can enter on your site in two ways.
The creative is ready.
Ads are live and entries are coming in.
Every entrant gets a welcome series.
Non-winners get a reason to buy.

topics.title: Line up creators
topics.why: People trust people. A creator showing your product to their followers before the sale warms up buyers who have never heard of you.
steps: Make a list of 10 small creators in your niche, with 2,000 to 50,000 followers. Look for people whose followers comment and ask questions.
Send each one a short, friendly message. Use the "Message to a creator" template in Helix's template library and change the [brackets].
Gift your product to the ones who say yes. Give each a personal code, such as their name plus 15, so you can see who brought sales. Offer a share of each sale they bring.
results: A list of 10 names with a link to each profile.
10 messages sent.
Each creator has the product, a code and a date to post before the sale.

topics.title: Find the worry behind the purchase
topics.why: Most stores talk about the problem everyone already mentions. The worry people feel but rarely say makes a message feel personal and stops the scroll. It might be looking silly, wasting money or letting someone down.
steps: Write the obvious problem your product solves in one line, for example "my dog pulls on the lead".
Under it, write what the customer feels but does not post about. Use your customer words list. For example: "I dread walking him past other dogs because people stare".
Write one thing they probably do not know yet that would change how they see the problem. For example: "pulling is usually a harness fit issue, not a training issue".
Turn each line into an ad hook or email subject line. Test the unspoken worry against your current best hook.
results: One plain line describing the obvious problem.
One to three unspoken worries, each in a customer's voice.
One surprising, true insight you can teach.
A new hook is live in a test next to your current winner.

topics.title: Turn one piece of content into ten
topics.why: Making new content every day burns owners out. One good piece, cut and reshaped for each channel, gives you a week of posts, emails and ad ideas.
steps: Pick one piece that already did well: your best video, a popular post, or a customer story. Check your Instagram or TikTok insights for the top post of the last 90 days.
Write out its main points, or get a transcript from your phone or an AI tool. List five short ideas inside it.
Turn each idea into one format. Make a short video, a carousel, a story poll, an email section and an ad hook.
Put them in your posting calendar across the next two weeks, one channel at a time.
results: One proven piece is chosen.
Five standalone ideas, each one sentence.
You have at least ten pieces from one starting point.
Two weeks of posts are scheduled.

topics.title: Social proof and reviews on social
topics.why: Social proof on social media turns curious visitors into buyers. Reviews, customer posts and kind replies to complaints all count.
steps: Turn your best reviews into an Instagram highlight, a carousel and a video where you read them out.
Ask happy customers to tag you. With permission, reshare their posts to Stories and save them to a highlight.
Keep shop ratings healthy where you sell through social shops. Reply to bad reviews kindly in public, then fix the problem in private.
results: Reviews are visible on your profile.
Customer posts fill a highlight.
Future customers see a calm, helpful reply.

topics.title: Plan before you build
topics.why: A store takes days to build and minutes to judge. Planning first means you build only what a buyer needs and know your numbers before the first sale. This takes about an hour.
steps: Write your one-line promise: who it is for and the result they get.
List your products with price, product cost and what one order costs you to send.
Choose one launch country (for example, where you live) and add more later.
Pick the cheapest Shopify plan that has the features you need. Most new stores start on Basic (check Shopify pricing).
Gather your logo, 4 to 8 photos per product and your returns rule. Also your ABN or EIN (US, if you have one) and a business bank account.
results: You can say in one sentence what you sell and who it is for.
You know your cost per order for each product.
You have one launch country.
You know your monthly platform cost. In October 2026, Basic was US$39 or A$56 a month, billed monthly.
Everything you need to build is in one folder.

topics.title: Domain and email
topics.why: Your domain is your web address. A store on its own domain looks more trustworthy than the free myshopify.com address. Emails from your own domain also land in inboxes more often.
steps: In Shopify, go to Settings > Domains. Buy a short domain that matches your brand, or connect one you own (see Shopify: domains).
Set it as the primary domain so myshopify.com redirects to it.
Set up a brand email like hello@yourbrand.com. Use it for support and as the sender in your email tool.
Send a test email to yourself.
results: The domain shows as connected in Settings.
Typing your domain opens your store.
Customer emails come from your own domain.
It lands in your inbox, not spam.

topics.title: Choose and set up a theme
topics.why: The theme is the design of your store. A fast, simple theme beats a fancy slow one. Always edit a copy, so you never break the live store.
steps: In Online Store > Themes, start with a free Shopify theme such as Horizon or Dawn (see Shopify: themes).
Click Duplicate on the theme and make all changes on the copy.
In Customize > Theme settings, set your logo, 2 to 3 colours and 1 to 2 fonts. Pick a button style.
Plan menus for desktop and mobile separately, with fewer, bigger links on phones.
results: A fast, supported theme is installed.
You are working on a copy, not the live theme.
Your store uses no more than 2 fonts and 3 main colours.
The mobile menu has 5 or fewer links.

topics.title: Build the home page
topics.why: The home page should answer three questions in a few seconds. What is this? Is it for me? Why should I trust it? Build the top first, then the sections below in a proven order.
steps: In the theme editor, add a promo bar with one short line. Use your shipping offer or a guarantee.
Set the header menu to your logo plus 4 to 5 links. For example: Shop, Bundles, Reviews, FAQ, About.
Add a banner with a photo of the product in use. Add your promise in one line and one button ("Shop now"). You can add a row of category tiles people swipe sideways on phones.
Below the banner, add these sections in this order. Use Add section in the theme editor for each.
Show your home page on a phone to someone new for 5 seconds.
results: The promo bar shows at the very top on every page.
The header is simple and uncluttered.
The top of the page says what you sell and gives one next step.
The home page has every section in a logical order.
They can say what you sell.

topics.title: The improvement system
topics.why: CRO (conversion rate optimisation) means getting more of your visitors to buy. A simple monthly loop beats random changes, because each fix is chosen for its likely payoff and then measured.
steps: Score each key page against the checklists in Lesson 14.2 and list every gap.
Rank each gap by how much it helps divided by how much work it is. Sort into quick wins, small builds and big builds.
Build the top quick wins using theme settings or apps first.
Measure with heatmaps, session recordings, funnel reports and A/B tests.
Add a monthly reminder to repeat the loop.
results: You have a list of missing items per page.
Your list is in priority order with quick wins at the top.
The quick wins are live. Pay for custom code only once an idea has proven it works.
Each change has a before and after number.
The next review is in your calendar.

topics.title: Page checklists
topics.why: Each page type has a short list of things shoppers expect. Missing items cost sales quietly. Above the fold means what people see before they scroll. On a phone that space is tiny, so it must work hard.
steps: Check the top of your home page on your phone, before you scroll. You want a promo bar ("Free shipping over $80") and a simple menu. Add a banner with one message and its own phone image. Add one clear button and a trust sign (star rating, customer count or press logo).
Check the lower part of the home page. Look for best sellers, categories, reasons to buy, reviews, your story, press and an email sign-up.

Check the top of each product page. You want the title and one line on what makes it different. Add the star rating, and the price with a compare-at price or bundle value. Add an offer ("Buy 2, save 10%"), a size or colour picker and Add to cart. Add a delivery estimate and trust badges (secure checkout, free returns).
Check the lower part of product pages. Look for reasons to buy, how to use it, photo reviews, FAQs, a comparison, guarantees and "goes well with" products.
Check collection pages. Look for filters you can combine with an easy reset, and sort by best selling. Add badges (new, best seller, low stock) and quick add to cart.

Check cart and checkout. You want a progress bar to free shipping or a gift, and one upsell spot. Add fast pay buttons (Shop Pay and the phone and online wallets Shopify offers), no surprise fees, and trust badges with policy links.
results: All five items are visible without scrolling on a phone.
Each section is present, in roughly that order.
All nine items show before scrolling on mobile.
Shoppers who scroll find answers to every common doubt.
Shoppers can narrow and buy from a collection in a few taps.
Checkout has no surprises and the fastest pay options.

topics.title: Accessibility basics
topics.why: Accessibility means everyone can use your store. That includes people who cannot see well or who use a keyboard instead of a mouse. Some fixes, like alt text, also help search engines understand your pages.
steps: Run your text and button colours through a free online contrast checker.
Add alt text to every product image in Shopify Products > [product] > Media. Alt text is a short description for screen readers.
Tab through your store with only the keyboard, from home page to checkout.
Check font sizes (at least 16px on phones is a common rule of thumb). Every form field needs a label, and every video needs captions.
results: Body text and buttons have strong contrast: at least WCAG AA, which is 4.5 to 1 for normal text (see web.dev: colour and contrast).
Every image has a short, descriptive alt text.
You can reach and use every link, button and form field.
Text is easy to read, forms are labelled and videos have captions.

topics.title: Say clearly what the customer gets
topics.why: The promise is the main result your product gives. If shoppers cannot repeat it back in one line, they will not buy. Reviews hold the exact words that sell.
steps: Read your 20 newest 4 and 5 star reviews. Copy the words customers use for the result they got.
Write one sentence for the problem or pain the product takes away, using the same words.
Write one sentence for how other people will see your customer differently after buying.
Turn it into one promise line.
results: You have a list of 5 to 10 phrases in customers' own words.
You have a pain sentence, for example "No more tangled cables in your bag".
You have a "how others see me" sentence.
The same promise line appears on the product page and in an ad.

topics.title: Give people reasons to believe you
topics.why: People do not buy until they believe the product will work for them. Each objection (a reason not to buy) that you answer with proof removes a barrier. Stores that answer objections on purpose can see conversion rise from the same visitors.
steps: List 20 reasons someone might not buy, using support emails, reviews, return notes and questions from your team.
Group them under six headings: price, quality, fit or size, trust, timing, and "do I need it?".
Write one proof for each worry. Use a review quote, a photo, a guarantee, a number or a demo video.
Add the answers to the product page FAQ, your ads and your welcome emails. Start with the biggest group.
results: You have a numbered list of 20 objections.
Every objection sits under one heading, and you can see which group is biggest.
Each objection has an answer you can show, not just claim.
The top objections are answered in at least three places shoppers see.

topics.title: Real scarcity
topics.why: Scarcity means there is a real reason the product may run out. That gives people a reason to act now. Honest scarcity builds trust; fake timers destroy it and can break consumer law. In Australia, after ACCC action, the Federal Court ordered a bedding seller to pay $15 million in 2026. Part of it was for a sale countdown timer that kept resetting (see ACCC: $15m penalty for misleading sale prices).
steps: Pick one honest way to show scarcity that fits your product. For example: a small batch with a number, or a preorder with a clear ship date. Or a colour for a short time, or low-stock alerts.
Write the reason in one sentence on the product page. For example: "Batch 4 of 6: 300 made, ships 14 November".
Set up a low-stock email for when stock drops below about 2 weeks of sales. Send it to people who viewed the product and to your best customers.
results: You have chosen one method you can stand behind.
Shoppers can see why it might not be available later.
An email goes out automatically when stock gets low.

topics.title: Sign-up forms
topics.why: A sign-up form (often a pop-up) asks visitors for their email or phone number. It feeds every flow and campaign you send. As a rule of thumb, a good form signs up 3 to 10 of every 100 people who see it. A weak one wastes your traffic.
steps: Pick one reward. Dollars off ($10 off) works if your orders are big, and percent off (10% off) if they are small. Or try a free gift, early access or a prize draw.
In your email or form app, build a form with steps. First a one-click question ("What are you shopping for?"), then email, then phone number.
Show it after about 5 to 8 seconds or 30% scroll. On computers, also show it when the mouse moves to leave. Hide it from people who already signed up.
If you sell to several regions, add location rules. Then each region sees offers and text sign-ups that suit it.
After 2 weeks, measure and improve.
Put a sign-up form inside a page too, not only as a pop-up.
results: Your form has one clear reason to sign up.
The form asks an easy question first, which raises completion (micro-commitment).
The form shows at the right moment and never to people already on the list.
Overseas visitors see an offer that fits them.
Over 3 in 100 people who see the form sign up, or a test is running to get there. As a rule of thumb, 6 to 10 is possible with a strong offer.
The form shows inside the page, and a test sign-up appears in your email list within a minute.

topics.title: The five core flows and extras
topics.why: A flow is a series of emails or texts that sends itself when someone does something. Five core flows earn money every day without you lifting a finger. Timings are in SOP 13.
steps: Set up the Welcome flow, triggered when someone joins your list.
Set up Browse abandonment, triggered when someone views a product but does not add to cart.
Set up Cart abandonment, triggered when someone adds to cart but does not start checkout.
Set up Checkout abandonment, triggered when someone starts checkout but does not pay.
Set up Post-purchase, triggered when someone buys.

Then add the extras one at a time. Win-back, back in stock, price drop, time to reorder, VIP and birthday. Also a clean-up flow (removing people who never open) and a review request. And a "you may also like" email after the first order.
results: New subscribers get your first email within minutes.
Browsers get a reminder of what they looked at.
Cart abandoners get a reminder within a few hours.
The highest-intent shoppers get a reminder within about an hour.
New buyers get thanks, how-to tips and a cross-sell.
Your flow list grows month by month.

topics.title: Writing emails that get clicks
topics.why: Emails that get clicks feel personal and have one clear job. Mixing plain founder emails with designed ones keeps your list interested.
steps: Alternate plain-text style emails from the founder (images are fine) with designed emails.
Use what people told you in forms to make emails fit them. That could be what they like, skin type or size.
Give each email one main button (call to action).
results: Your next four campaigns include at least one founder-style email.
Different subscribers see different product picks.
Every email has one obvious next step.

topics.title: Your yearly sales calendar
topics.why: A year of sales works best as a rhythm. Customers learn when to look, and you are never rushing. Four kinds of promotion cover the year. Deep discounts belong only to clearing slow stock, and only as a last resort.
steps: Pick a regular day and time for new products, like the first Thursday of each month at 7pm. Put the next 6 on your calendar.
Add gift days and cultural moments (Mother's Day, Valentine's Day). Offer a picked selection, not a store-wide discount.
Choose 3 to 4 big sales peaks for the year, with Black Friday usually the biggest.
For slow stock, plan gentle tools first: a free gift with purchase, bundles, VIP codes or gift cards.
results: Your release dates are set and repeat monthly.
Each event has a product selection planned.
Your peaks are on the calendar with dates.
Slow stock has a clearing plan that avoids deep discounts.

topics.title: Launch phases
topics.why: A launch has four phases, and each needs its own message. Skipping the build-up or the follow-up leaves most of the sales on the table.
steps: Before launch, tease the product and open a waitlist and early-access sign-up.
On launch day, give VIPs (best customers) access first, then everyone.
Mid-launch, release something new for 24 hours, like a new colour or a bundle.
After launch, share reviews, results and restock news.
results: People are signing up before the product is out.
VIPs get a head start and feel looked after.
The launch gets a second spike.
Proof keeps sales going after the launch week.

topics.title: The big sale, step by step
topics.why: A big sale is a project with seven parts, from the target to the shipping cut-offs. Planning each part in order is what makes a sale profitable and repeatable.
steps: Set the target: last year's sales for this event times your growth rate. Check it against list size, budget and stock.
Build the offer: a main offer and free gift levels (spend $100, get a gift). Add something new mid-sale and a VIP extra. Check your margin at every level.
Pick a theme: a name, a look and a message that stand out from competitors.
Plan the ad budget per day for each part of the sale (hype, launch, middle, finish). Also plan the split between normal and sale campaigns.
List the ads needed for each phase and audience (cold, warm, hot). Plan emails and texts too.
Get the site ready: sale pages and banners, and no site changes for 2 weeks before. Test every discount code.
results: You have a sales target you can resource.
Every offer level still makes money.
The sale has a name and a visual style.
Every sale day has a planned budget.
Creative and messages are planned for every phase.
The site is ready and stable before launch.

topics.title: Plan your offer and order stock
topics.why: Stock takes weeks to arrive, and an offer you rush is often one that loses money. Deciding early keeps you calm and keeps your profit.
steps: Open Numbers in Helix. Write down your profit on one order before ads. Helix shows it in Profit setup.
Pick one simple offer. Keep the discount smaller than half of that profit, so each sale still pays for its ad. A free gift or a bundle often costs you less than a big discount.
Look at how many of your best seller you sell on a normal day. Plan for about three times that on each sale day. Order now so it arrives at least two weeks early.
results: You have one number, such as "$18 profit per order before ads".
One offer written down, such as "15% off everything" or "free tote over $60".
Your stock order is placed, with an arrival date before the sale.

topics.title: Set up a discount code in Shopify
topics.why: Get a code ready, tested and set to start and stop by itself. Then there is no late-night rush on the big day.
steps: In Shopify admin, open Discounts in the left menu. Press Create discount.
Pick Amount off products for a discount on some products, or Amount off orders for the whole cart.
Under Method, keep Discount code. Type your code, such as BFCM26. Short codes are easier to type.
Under Value, pick Percentage and type your number, such as 15.
Under Active dates, set the start date and time, then press Set end date and add the end. Use your store's time zone.
Press Save. Then place a test order with the code (you can cancel and refund it) to check it works.
results: A box asks you to pick a discount type.
The discount form opens.
Your code shows at the top of the form.
The summary on the right says "15% off".
The summary shows the start and end dates.
The code works at checkout and the discount is right.

topics.title: Dress your store, warm up and write your emails
topics.why: Shoppers decide fast. Get the store ready for the day and write your emails. Then every visit has a clear path to buy.
steps: Add a homepage banner with the offer and the end date.
Make one collection for the event, like "Gifts under $50". Add an announcement bar at the top of every page.
Write a short gift guide: three to six products, one line each on who it suits.
Warm up your audience. Post about the coming sale, and ask people to join your email list for early access.
Write three emails: "It starts tomorrow", "It's on" and "Last day". Use the sale email templates in Helix.
results: The first thing a visitor sees is the offer.
One click from the banner takes people to the collection.
The guide is live and linked from the banner.
New sign-ups each day before the sale.
Three emails are scheduled in your email tool.

topics.title: Sold out? Pre-orders and back-in-stock lists
topics.why: A sold-out page with no next step loses the sale forever. A back-in-stock alert or a pre-order keeps the shopper. It also tells you how much to order next.
steps: Install a back-in-stock app, or use the one in your email tool. Turn on a "Notify me" button for sold-out products.
Write a short email for when stock returns. Say it is back, show the product, and add one button.
For products with a firm delivery date, turn on pre-orders. Show the ship date clearly on the product page and at checkout.
Take payment only if you are sure of the date. If you are not sure, collect a waitlist instead.
Count sign-ups for each product. Add them to your next order size.
results: Sold-out pages show a "Notify me" button instead of a dead end.
People on the list get an email the moment stock arrives.
Shoppers can buy now and know when it will ship.
You never hold money for stock that might not come.
Your next order matches real demand.

topics.title: Collect your customers' own words
topics.why: People buy when they read their own thoughts back. Copy written in your customers' words beats copy written in yours, in ads, on product pages and in emails.
steps: Open a blank document called "Customer words". Copy in 30 phrases from your 5-star reviews and your 1 to 3-star reviews. Add phrases from customer emails and any rival reviews on Amazon or Google.
Sort them under four headings. What annoyed them before? What were they afraid of? What did they hope for? What surprised them after buying?
Send your last 50 customers a one-question email. Ask: "What nearly stopped you buying?" Add the answers to the list.
Rewrite the first line of your best product page and one ad. Use a phrase from the list, word for word where you can.
results: You have 30 real phrases, each with where it came from.
Each heading has at least five phrases.
You have at least 10 new answers in their words.
One page and one ad now open with a real customer phrase.

topics.title: A weekly story email
topics.why: Sale-only emails train people to wait for discounts. A short weekly email with a story, a useful idea and one product keeps your brand in mind. It sells at full price.
steps: Pick one fixed day and time for your weekly email.
Write it in four parts. A subject that sounds like a friend. A short story from the week (a customer, a product choice, a mistake). The lesson in one line. One product that fits.
Use a phrase from your customer words list in the subject or first line.
After four weeks, compare clicks and revenue per email with your sale emails.
results: A recurring slot is in your calendar.
A 150 to 250-word email in that order.
The email speaks in your customers' words.
You know what the weekly email earns.

topics.title: Answer the top buying questions by email
topics.why: Most people who sign up do not buy straight away because a question is holding them back. Answering those questions in a short email series removes the blockers one at a time.
steps: List the five questions people ask most before they buy. For example: sizing, delivery time, returns, how it compares, and is it worth the price.
Write one short email per question. Give a straight answer, proof (a review or photo) and a link to the best product.
Add them to your welcome flow after the first email, two days apart.
results: Five questions ranked by how often they come up.
Five emails drafted.
New subscribers get the answers before they lose interest.

topics.title: Why revenue is the wrong scoreboard
topics.why: Revenue (all the money customers paid you) feels like success. But it does not tell you what you kept. A $5,000 day can still lose money once you pay for ads, products and shipping. Ad platforms also each claim the same sale, so their totals add up to more sales than you really had. This lesson gets you a real starting point so you can see the gap for yourself.
steps: Find last month's sales in your store.

Add up last month's ad spend from every platform and write down the total. In Meta, go to Ads Manager > Campaigns, pick last month and read the Amount spent column. In Google Ads, read Campaigns > Cost.
Guess how much profit you made last month. Write it down as one dollar number before you do any maths.
Save the three numbers somewhere easy to find. A note on your phone works, or the notes field in Helix Settings.
results: You have one dollar figure for last month's net sales written in a note or on paper.
You have one total ad spend figure for last month.
A guessed profit figure sits next to your sales and ad spend.

You can find the note later. At the end of this module you check your guess. You compare it with your real contribution profit (sales minus order costs and ads). You also compare it with net profit (what is left after bills).

topics.title: Your cost drivers
topics.why: Cost drivers are your average costs, and they are what turn sales into profit. Get them roughly right once and every profit number in Helix becomes trustworthy. You set them up in about 30 minutes and check them every 3 months.
steps: Work out your product cost %. If your plan has it, use Analytics > Reports > Gross profit by product (fill in "Cost per item" first). Or take your top 10 sellers. Divide each one's landed cost (price paid plus freight and duty) by its selling price.

Work out your shipping and packing cost per order. Take last month's bills from your carrier or warehouse (a 3PL is a company that stores and ships for you). Divide by the number of orders you shipped.
Add packaging per order (boxes, mailers, tape, inserts) by dividing last month's packaging spend by orders.
Find your payment fee %. In Shopify, go to Settings > Payments, click Manage under Shopify Payments and read Standard rates. Or divide last month's total fees (on your payouts page) by sales.

List every fixed cost for one month. Include staff and helpers, a fair wage for yourself, software and apps, rent, insurance and accounting. Add loan interest and any marketing that is not ad spend (photo shoots, free product for creators, agency fees).
Save your fixed costs in Helix.
results: You have one percentage. For many online stores it sits somewhere between 20% and 40%.
You have a dollar amount per order, for example $9.
You have a second per-order figure, often $0.50 to $2.
You have a percentage, often about 2% to 3.5% once the 30 cent fee per order is counted. It depends on plan, country, card mix and buy now pay later (see Shopify: payout fees and card rates).
You have one monthly total for fixed costs.
The Dashboard's net profit now takes off a daily share of your fixed costs. That share is your monthly total divided by 30.4.

topics.title: Three kinds of constraint
topics.why: A constraint is the one thing limiting your profit right now. Fixing anything else first wastes time and money. Many stores are short of sales even when the owner thinks they have an "ads problem".
steps: Open the Dashboard on Month. Write down orders, net sales, MER and contribution margin (contribution profit divided by net sales).
Match them to one of the three kinds in the table below. Throughput means not enough sales. Efficiency means costs are too high. Capacity means you cannot keep up with orders.
Write the constraint at the top of your decision log and keep it there until it is fixed.
results: You have four numbers to diagnose from.
You have named one constraint.
Every change you make this month can be checked against that one constraint.

topics.title: The five situations
topics.why: The same tactic can help one store and hurt another. Your scorecard puts you in one of five situations, and each has a different next move. Picking the right one stops you scaling a leaky store or cutting a healthy one.
steps: Check your net profit % for the last 30 days on the Dashboard. If it is 10% or more, your profit is healthy. Grow, and win every customer you can serve at a profit.

If profit is under 10%, find the cost share that is too high. Fixed costs heavy: grow carefully, because doubling sales halves their share. Variable costs heavy: pause growth and fix cost per order first. Marketing heavy: MER is high, so find where buyers drop out before you touch the ads.
If every number is borderline, follow this order: fix MER first, then VCR (order costs), then grow.
results: You know whether you are in the healthy group.
You have picked one of the three cost situations.
You have a written order of work for the next month.

topics.title: Decision rules: scale, hold, refresh, kill
topics.why: Four decisions cover every ad: scale, hold, refresh or kill. In Helix these show as Spend more, Wait, New ads needed and Stop. Using fixed rules removes emotion from the call.
steps: Open Your ads in Helix and read the verdict next to each campaign.
Check each verdict against the rules in the table below.
Act on one verdict today and write it in your decision log.
results: Every campaign shows one of the four verdicts.
You agree with the verdict or know why not.
One change is made and recorded.

topics.title: Scaling challenge
topics.why: A scaling challenge is a planned 2 to 4 week push to spend more. If you have new ads ready and a loss limit set, even a failed test teaches you. It shows what is holding you back.
steps: Prepare 6 to 10 new ads before you start.
Write down the most you are willing to lose.
Raise the budget a little.
Hold each new level for 10 to 14 days.
Read the result.
results: Fresh ads are ready to add as frequency rises.
You have a dollar limit that ends the challenge.
You can see whether new spend is finding new people.
MER has time to settle at each level.
You have a clear next action, whether the challenge worked or not.

topics.title: Reporting that leads to decisions
topics.why: A report is only useful if it leads to a decision. Four questions do that; dashboards with 40 numbers do not.
steps: Start each report with what happened. Show sales, contribution profit and MER (total ad spend as a share of total sales) against target.
Add why: the one or two biggest causes with evidence.
Add what you did this period and the next three actions with an owner and a date each.
results: Three numbers open every report.
Every change has a reason.
The report ends in decisions.

topics.title: Target ROAS
topics.why: Target ROAS tells Google how many dollars of sales you want for each $1 of ads. Set it from your break-even, not a guess, and change it gently.
steps: Work out break-even ROAS: 1 divided by (1 minus VCR, your order costs as a share of sales). With VCR at 45%, that is about 1.82.
In the campaign's Bidding settings, set target ROAS above break-even with room for profit. For example, 2.4 if break-even is 1.82.
Change targets in small steps, about 10% at a time (a common rule of thumb). Wait a week or two before the next change.
results: You have your break-even ROAS.
Google bids to a target that leaves profit.
Bidding stays stable while you tune it.

topics.title: Which products to push: a monthly product check
topics.why: Not every product deserves your ad money. A healthy store total can hide one product that loses money on every order. A monthly check of profit per product shows which ones to push, which to test more and which to stop. It takes about 30 minutes.
steps: In Shopify, open Analytics > Reports and pick the sales by product report (called Total sales by product). Set the dates to last month.

For each product, work out the profit from one sale before ads: the price people really paid, minus product cost, the shipping you pay, packaging and payment fees (Lesson 1.2 lists them). Multiply by units sold.

Add last month's ad spend for each product. Use campaigns or ad sets that promote one product. For mixed or catalog campaigns, split the spend by each product's share of the sales they brought in. Then take ad spend away from profit before ads.
Put each product into one of the four boxes in the table below, then do the action for that box. "Good return" means profit after ads is above zero and the return beats your break-even ROAS.
Move ad budget towards the "good return" boxes in your next weekly review, and save the table so you can compare next month.
results: One row per product with units sold and net sales.
A profit-before-ads number for each product. For example: sells for $50, costs $15 to make, $8 to ship and $1.50 in fees, so $25.50 each. 120 sold is $3,060.
Each product has ad spend, profit after ads, and a return (sales divided by ad spend).
Every product has a box and a next step. For example: "low spend, good return: make new ads and give it more budget".
More of your spend goes to products that pay it back, and you can see the trend month to month.

topics.title: Segments
topics.why: A segment is a group of people on your list who share something. Sending to the right segment keeps emails out of spam folders and makes each message more useful.
steps: In your email app, make groups. Use people who engaged in the last 30, 60 and 90 days, buyers, repeat buyers and VIPs.
Add window shoppers (looked recently, never bought), lapsed buyers (used to buy, stopped) and product-interest segments.
Send most campaign emails to the engaged 60 or 90 day segment.
results: The segments show live counts.
You can target each stage of the customer journey.
Open rates rise and spam complaints fall.

topics.title: After the sale
topics.why: After a sale there is always a slow time, because some people just bought earlier than they would have. As a rule of thumb, the dip takes back some of the extra sales, not all of them. How you handle it decides how many new buyers you keep. A short review makes the next event better.
steps: Turn normal campaigns back up in steps over a week, not all at once.
Check that new buyers are getting your post-purchase emails.
Review sales against target, MER, new customers and stock left, and write down one thing to improve.
Wait 7 days after the sale ends before you write down final numbers. Ad apps keep adding late sales for about a week.
Plan the next 2 to 4 weeks without a new discount. Show full-price news, like a new product or a best-seller story. Nudge new buyers towards a second order.
results: Campaigns recover without a spending shock.
New customers get thanks and how-to tips.
You have a short review with one improvement for next time.
Your review uses numbers from 7 days after the sale, not the first morning.
A short plan for the weeks after the sale, with no discount in it.

topics.title: Review the results
topics.why: Write next year's plan the week after this one. You will still remember what happened.
steps: In Numbers, add up the event days: sales, orders, ad spend and profit.
Write three things that worked and three you would change.
Send a thank-you email to everyone who bought. Use the "Thank-you after a sale" template.
results: One line with the totals.
A short note you can read next year.
Buyers feel looked after, and more of them come back.

topics.title: Range planning
topics.why: Your range is the set of products you sell. Planning it on purpose puts your cash into styles that earn, and lets you test new ideas small before committing.
steps: Choose the categories that earn the most and fit your brand. Use last year's sales and margin by category.
Track every style in one table. Note the launch date, units sold, sell-through % (share of stock sold), margin and whether you will reorder.
Order small first runs of new styles and reorder winners quickly.
Write a range plan: styles per category and price points. Note how many are new and how many are core (always in stock).
Forecast core products from their sales history and new products from similar past launches.
results: You have a short list of focus categories.
Every style has a row you update monthly.
New styles are tested with little cash at risk.
You have a one-page range plan.
Each product has a forecast based on evidence.

topics.title: Your payment mix and what it really costs
topics.why: Each way to pay has its own fee, payout speed and risk. The fee on the price page is rarely the whole cost.
steps: Download last month's payout reports from each provider (Shopify Payments, any wallet or buy now pay later provider).
For each provider, divide total fees by the sales it processed.
Add hidden costs: currency conversion on withdrawal, fixed per-order fees on small orders and fees kept on refunds.
Enter your blended fee rate (all fees divided by all sales) in Helix as payment fees.
Keep the ways to pay that customers use. As a rule of thumb, drop any under about 2% of orders that costs much more than cards.
Check each provider's fee page once a year.
results: You have one report per provider.
You have a real fee rate per provider.
Your fee rates include everything.
Helix profit uses your real fees.
Your payment list is lean.
Fee rises never surprise you.

topics.title: Do you need a 3PL yet?
topics.why: Packing orders yourself is cheap at first and expensive later, because your hours stop going into growth. A 3PL is a warehouse company that stores and ships for you. It makes sense when packing takes more of your week than selling does.
steps: For one normal week, write down how many orders you sent. Note the hours spent packing, labelling and dropping off.
Work out your cost per order today. Add packaging, labels, postage, and your time at a fair hourly rate.
Ask at least 3 warehouses for a price on the same sample month. Give orders per month, units per order, number of products, carton sizes, and pallets or shelves of stock.
Compare the full monthly bill, not just pick and pack. Include receiving, storage (per pallet, shelf or cubic metre) and packaging. Add monthly minimums, set-up, returns and busy-season extras.
Ask each warehouse for a sample invoice from a client of similar size.
Ask 3 service questions. What is the daily order cut-off time? What error rate do they measure? What do they do when they make a mistake?
results: You have orders per week and packing hours per week.
You have one true cost per order, including your time.
You have 3 quotes for the same workload.
You can see the real total for each quote.
You can see fees the price sheet leaves out.
You know how reliable each warehouse is.

topics.title: GST: register, charge and lodge
topics.why: GST (goods and services tax) is 10% on most local sales once you are registered. The money you collect is held for the ATO (the tax office), not earned by you, so set it aside.
steps: Check your GST turnover (this month plus the last 11). Register within 21 days of reaching $75,000. Or register as soon as you expect to reach it within 12 months (see ATO: GST).
Once registered, show prices to local customers with GST included and issue tax invoices.
Open a separate bank account and each week move one eleventh of GST-inclusive sales into it.
Send in your BAS (business activity statement) on time. Quarterly due dates are 28 October, 28 February, 28 April and 28 July (see ATO: BAS due dates).
Claim GST credits on business costs that include GST, like local stock and services. Keep the tax invoices.
In Helix Settings, keep My prices include GST/VAT on Use my country's default (or Yes if the sales you type include GST).
results: You know whether you must register.
Checkout prices include GST.
The GST bill is already saved when it is due.
Dates are on your calendar. Lodging online may add two weeks, except for the December quarter.
Your BAS includes your credits.
Helix profit leaves GST out.

topics.title: Choose your structure and your helpers
topics.why: Your business structure changes how you pay tax and what you are personally liable for. A good accountant pays for themselves, while a poor bookkeeper can cost you a year of clean-up.
steps: Learn the two roles. A bookkeeper keeps records up to date each week or month. An accountant or tax agent does tax returns, gives tax advice and helps you plan.
Ask every candidate the same three questions.
Choose a fixed monthly fee with a written list of what is included. Also list what costs extra, like tax returns or catch-up work.
Ask for read-only access to your books from day one and a short monthly summary.
Review your structure with your accountant once profit is steady.
results: You know which helper you need for what.
You can compare candidates on the same answers.
There are no surprise bills.
You can see your books any time.
Your structure still suits the business.

topics.title: Lock down every account
topics.why: One stolen password can cost more than a bad month of sales. Thieves target ad accounts because they can spend your money fast. An hour of lock-down work closes most doors.
steps: List every account the business needs. That is email and domain, Shopify, Meta, Google and TikTok. Add your email tool, payment providers, bank and the place you bought your domain.
Turn on two-factor authentication (a second check after your password) on each one. Use an authenticator app or security key, not text messages.
Store a different long password for every account in a password manager.
Save each account's backup codes offline where a trusted person can reach them.
Make at least 2 trusted people full admins on Meta, Google and Shopify, each with their own login.
Every quarter, tidy who has access.
results: You have one list of every account.
Every account asks for a second check at login.
No password is reused.
You can get back in if you lose your phone.
No one shares a login and no single person can lock you out.
The access check is on your Helix calendar.

topics.title: Is there demand?
topics.why: Expanding to a country with no demand burns cash on shipping, ads and setup. A quick check of your own data shows where people already want what you sell.
steps: In Shopify, open Analytics > Reports > Total sales by billing location and Sessions by location. List your top 5 countries outside home for the last 12 months.
Check search demand for your product type in each (Google Keyword Planner, set to that country).
Check if rivals already sell there. See where your social followers come from (Instagram Insights > Total followers > Top locations).
Pick the country that already buys from you most.
results: You have a ranked list of countries with orders and visits.
Each country has a monthly search volume.
Each country has a competition and audience note.
You have one first country to expand to.

topics.title: Your first hire
topics.why: Your first hire should give you back hours. Pick work that does not need you.
steps: For two weeks, log every task and its time. Mark each one: only I can do it, someone could do it with a checklist, or it should stop.
Group the checklist tasks into one role, such as customer service, order problems, product uploads and reporting.
Write the role as outcomes, for example "every customer email answered within one business day".
Give shortlisted people a small paid trial task that matches the real work.
Agree terms in writing: hours or deliverables, rate, notice, confidentiality and that their work belongs to you.
Check whether the person is an employee or contractor based on the real arrangement, not the label.
results: You have a task log with every task marked.
You have a first role worth about 10 hours a week or more.
Success is measurable.
You see real work before hiring.
A signed agreement exists.
You know which rules apply.

topics.title: Personal operating basics
topics.why: You are the most important part of the business. How you sleep, plan and handle messages decides the quality of every other decision. Seven basics protect your best hours.
steps: Set a fixed bedtime and wake time for weekdays and protect them.
Block your focus time in the calendar first each week, then fit meetings around it.
Check messages at set times (for example 9am, 1pm, 4pm) and turn off notifications you do not need.
Give every meeting an agenda, one owner and a decision.
Work in focused blocks of 25 or 45 minutes on one thing at a time.
Work out what your hour is worth, for example target yearly profit divided by working hours. Hand off work worth less than that.
results: You sleep about the same hours every night.
Your calendar has protected focus blocks.
You are not pulled away all day.
Meetings end with a decision, often early.
You finish deep tasks without switching.
You have a list of tasks to delegate.

topics.title: Set up AI helpers for daily work
topics.why: AI assistants (chat AI tools) work much better when they know about your business. A project with your context turns generic answers into useful ones.
steps: Create a project in your AI assistant. Most chat AI tools have a project (or similar) space where you can add files and instructions. Before you upload anything, check the tool's data settings and turn off using your chats for training if you can.
Upload your brand core (Module 3), customer profiles, offers and costs (Module 1). Add your SOPs and past winning ads and emails.
Update the files whenever something changes.
results: You have an empty project for your store.
The project holds your business context.
Answers stay current with your business.

topics.title: The stack by need and stage
topics.why: The right tools depend on your stage. You may be just starting or have steady weekly sales (stage 1). Or you run several channels with real ad spend (stage 2). Buying tools too early slows your site and drains cash.
steps: Decide your stage. Day one is just starting. Stage 1 is steady sales every week. Stage 2 is several channels and real ad spend.
For each need in the table below, compare what you use now with the suggestion for your stage.
Cancel tools that are ahead of your stage and add only the one gap that matters most.
results: You know which column of the table below applies to you.
You have a list of gaps and of tools you do not need yet.
Your stack fits your stage.

topics.title: Choose the few numbers that lead
topics.why: Sales and profit tell you what already happened. A few leading numbers warn you a week early, while you can still act.
steps: Pick five to seven numbers. Take at least two results (net profit, sales). Add three early-warning ones (sessions, add-to-cart rate, conversion rate, cost per order, email sign-ups).
Fill in each number for the last four weeks, from Helix or your reports.
Set a target for each from that history. Aim a little higher than your average, not a guess.
Drop any number you cannot fill in within two minutes. Replace it with one you can.
results: A short list of five to seven numbers.
Four weeks of history for every number.
Each number has a realistic target.
Every number is quick to update each week.
